newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Ex-premier to challenge president in Armenia poll.
newsitem.headline: Ex-premier to challenge president in Armenia poll.

text.p: Armenia's presidential election, a fortnight away, is shaping up as a tough, two-horse race between current leader Levon Ter-Petrosyan and former prime minister Vazgen Manukyan.

Three of seven candidates who had qualified for the ballot withdrew late on Saturday and lined up behind Manukyan, who served as the country's first prime minister in 1990-91 and later as defence minister.

Political observers say another, Ashot Manucharyan of the party of Science and Industry and the Citizens' Union party, is likely to drop out too as opposition groups form a single right-wing front to face the centre-right Ter-Petrosyan.

That leaves Ter-Petrosyan, a Syrian-born son of an Armenian Communist who has been president since independence in 1991, and the 50-year-old Manukyan as the only serious contenders for the five-year term.
Communist candidate Sergei Badalyan says he will remain in the race but he is not expected to garner much support.
Some 2.4 million of the nation's three and a half million citizens are eligible to cast ballots in this rocky country sandwiched between Turkey, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Iran.

Several hundred thousand Armenian emmigrants and citizens abroad can cast ballots at embassies. If no candidate gets a majority in the September 22 contest, there will be a runoff between the top two finishers.
Ter-Petrosyan, a former academic, has dominated Armenia's political landscape for years and is campaigning on themes of stability and continued economic reforms which have begun to bear fruit.

Manukyan is hitting populist themes hard, promising in speeches to raise real wages up to 10 times. He criticises the president for not doing enough to speed privatisation and pledges to revive heavy industry.
His words find a ready audience in Armenia, where most people remain on the breadline in the wake of the break-up of the Soviet Union.

Armenia more than any other former Soviet republic was reliant on the rest of the Union for energy imports for survival, importing natural gas that accounted for up to 90 percent of its electricity needs in winter months.
The lack of power has become a symbol of the nation's plight. Most residents get by with only a few hours of electricity a day and industry has been badly hit.
Officials were forced earlier this year to reopen a nuclear power plant standing along a fault line closed after a devasating 1988 earthquake which killed 10,000 people.
Opinion polls, while notoriously inaccurate in Armenia, generally suggest that Ter-Petrosyan is in for a tough battle.

Armenia has been at war for eight years with neighbouring Moslem Azerbaijan over the disputed region of Nagorno-Karabakh. Although a ceasefire has held for two years and Armenia has effectively won the war for the time being, the conflict hangs over the country's future like a cloud.
Ter-Petrosyan says Azeri guarantees of wide autonomy for the Armenian-populated enclave are insufficient, while Manukyan takes a hard line, insisting that Azerbaijan recognise its independence.
